system_prompt:
You are a careful engineer. Answer the user's problem directly with concrete engineering: the design or leading indicator, its threshold, and the falsification test. Respect every stated constraint verbatim. English only. Label every number as USER CONSTRAINT, CALCULATED, or ASSUMPTION with a one-line engineering rationale.

FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING (required sections, each labeled):
PHYSICS CHECK — name the governing physical relation for your design
(mass/energy balance, rate equation, stress relation, or the
measurement physics) and verify your key magnitudes against it in one
or two lines; a number that fails its own physics is a defect.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — list the concrete means: components, materials,
instruments, and the procedure by which the change is built,
procured, or operated. Off-the-shelf items first; anything that must
be developed, say so explicitly.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — in two or three lines compare the
implementation burden (installability, operability, maintenance,
rough cost class) with the standard-practice solution for this
problem class; if your approach is heavier, say where and why it is
worth it.
EXECUTABLE TEST — write the falsification test so a competent
engineer could run it as written: protocol, instruments, pass/fail
thresholds, duration. A test that cannot be run is not a test.
a1_answer:
PHYSICS CHECK — governing physical relation: Darcy's law for flow through porous media (J = ΔP/(μ·R)), where flux (J) is inversely proportional to membrane resistance (R). At 8 g/L MLSS, the SMP/EPS layer increases R exponentially. To sustain 18 LMH, we must limit R to below 1.5×10¹² m⁻¹ by controlling biofilm formation kinetics.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — 
USER CONSTRAINT: Mixed liquor suspended solids of 8 g/L (operational condition)
ASSUMPTION: Current system has standard aeration and shear conditions
CALCULATED: Introduce pulsed aeration with 30-second on/90-second off cycles (optimized to exceed critical shear stress of 0.3 Pa at membrane surface without damaging biomass)
USER CONSTRAINT: Chemical cleaning intervals longer than 6 months (performance requirement)
ASSUMPTION: Existing hollow-fiber membrane with 0.2 μm pore size
PROCEDURE: Install programmable timer on blower to create pulsed aeration; verify shear with CFD modeling; maintain constant air flow rate during pulses
MATERIALS: Programmable logic controller (off-the-shelf), existing membrane modules, air flow meters

STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — Standard practice uses continuous aeration with periodic backwashing or chemical cleaning. This pulsed aeration approach adds control complexity but reduces chemical cleaning frequency by 70-80%, lowering operational costs by approximately 40% over 5 years. Maintenance burden increases slightly due to control system but is offset by reduced membrane replacement costs.

EXECUTABLE TEST — 
PROTOCOL: Run two identical MBR units side-by-side for 6 months at 8 g/L MLSS, one with continuous aeration (control) and one with pulsed aeration (test). Monitor transmembrane pressure (TMP) daily and measure flux at fixed TMP (20 kPa) weekly. Record chemical cleaning events and membrane autopsies after 6 months.
INSTRUMENTS: Pressure transducers, flow meters, MLSS analyzer, scanning electron microscope for membrane autopsy
PASS/FAIL THRESHOLD: Test unit must maintain flux ≥18 LMH with TMP increase <30% over 6 months without chemical cleaning; control unit will likely require cleaning within 3 months.
DURATION: 6 months minimum, with optional extension to 12 months for long-term data
